name: Horse domestication on the lower Volga-Don steppe
summary: Herders of the lower Volga-Don steppe bred the horse lineage that spread across Eurasia from about 2200 BCE and from which all modern domestic horses descend.
description: Analysis of 273 ancient horse genomes places the ancestors of modern domestic horses in the western Eurasian steppes, especially the lower Volga-Don, in the late fourth and early third millennia BC. From around 2200 BC breeders produced these horses in large numbers; they reached Anatolia, the lower Danube, Bohemia and Central Asia by about 2200 to 2000 BC and replaced nearly all other horse populations. The earlier domestic horses of Botai, about 3500 BC, are a separate lineage that is not ancestral to modern breeds.

impact.note: The paper shows this lineage replacing nearly all others across Eurasia and opens by saying horse domestication 'fundamentally transformed long-range mobility and warfare'; riding and draught horses then changed how most societies travelled, fought, herded and hauled for some four thousand years, and chariotry, cavalry, courier systems and horse-powered farming and machinery rest on it. The later consequences are scored on the general view, not on the cited paper.

date.label: from around 2200 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Ancient genomes show a turnover of the horse population in which breeders produced large stocks of the modern domestic lineage (DOM2), whose homeland the paper places in the lower Volga-Don, from around 2200 BC.

evidence.supports: Altogether, our genomic data uncover a high turnover of the horse population in which past breeders produced large stocks of DOM2 horses to supply increasing demands for horse-based mobility from around 2200 bc

date.label: c. 2200–2000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Horses of the modern domestic lineage spread out of their core region and first reached Anatolia, the lower Danube, Bohemia and Central Asia by about 2200 to 2000 BC.

evidence.supports: The globalization stage started later, when DOM2 horses dispersed outside their core region, first reaching Anatolia, the lower Danube, Bohemia and Central Asia by approximately 2200 to 2000 bc

date.label: from about 2000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Modern domestic horses expanded rapidly across Eurasia from about 2000 BC and in time replaced almost all other local horse populations.

evidence.supports: This reveals that modern domestic horses ultimately replaced almost all other local populations as they expanded rapidly across Eurasia from about 2000 bc

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The Botai evidence (bridling, milking and corralling, about 3500 BCE) is a separate community and an earlier domestic lineage; it should have its own record under this concept.
The lower Volga-Don coordinates are a rough centre of the area, not a site.
When this lineage was first ridden or herded, as opposed to bred in large numbers, is not dated by the source; the claims of Yamnaya riding and of no knowledge of donkeys were not checked.

research.note: The paper calls the Botai horses the earliest known domestic horses and shows they are not ancestral to this lineage, but it does not say whether the Volga-Don breeders knew of horse keeping at Botai or of domestic donkeys.
